newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir inching towards normalcy after poll.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir inching towards normalcy after poll.

text.p: The vast Mughal gardens on the edge of Srinagar's Dal Lake are alive with the sound of laughter and the shouts of children after six years of federal rule.
The massive chinar trees at Nishat Garden in the Kashmiri summer capital tower over relaxed knots of Indian paramilitary troops picnicking on the lawns with their families.
The fountains are not sprinkling yet, and the stepped pools are still dry. But it may be only a matter of time before everything is working again.
India's Jammu and Kashmir state has just concluded its first local elections in a decade. New Delhi imposed direct rule over the Himalayan state after a separatist revolt flared in 1990.
The insurgency, in which more than than 20,000 people have died, has severely hurt the state's tourism industry, battered the economy and destroyed infrastructure.

"This is the first time I've been able to bring my family here," said a Border Security Force trooper, seated on the grass in Nishat Garden, surrounded by his wife and playing children. "Things have really improved now."

The soldier, who did not want to be identified, said security forces had driven the separatist guerrillas out of most areas of Srinagar. "That's why I can bring my children here without fears," he added.

A measure of normalcy may be returning -- restaurant owners say many more Kashmiri women are venturing out unaccompanied than at any time in the last six years -- but security chiefs are taking no chances.
"The militants are down but not out," said the chief of one of the paramilitary forces stationed in the northern state. "I have advised that there should be no reduction in forces for six months."
There are dozens of Kashmiri separatist guerrilla groups fighting for self-determination or closer ties to Islamic Pakistan.
Many Kashmiris hope things will improve under the new state government of the moderate National Conference party, which swept the local polls in September.
But separatist political parties, which boycotted the polls, have rejected the new government as a "puppet" regime installed by the federal government.
Security forces say the party's charismatic leader and new chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, will be a prime target for militants.
"Farooq Abdullah is going to be one of the top targets for the militants," police chief Mahender Sabharwal told Reuters. "We will have to make tight arrangements for his security."
Abdullah, well-known for his pro-India views, has said he would deal firmly with the rebels, but he remains open to dialogue with separatist political leaders.
Militants acted only a few hours after Abdullah returned to Srinagar, the state's summer capital, from New Delhi to begin forming a government.

Seven of his National Conference supporters were shot dead by a group of unidentified militants who stormed into their homes in Sumbal, 35 km (20 miles) north of Srinagar, and fired indiscriminately on the occupants, police said.
The area is a hotbed of pro-India militancy. Security officials say at least three pro-India militias are helping them fight separatist militants.
India put an estimated 200,000 security personnel into the Himalayan state in preparation for the elections.
Twenty-one political activists died in election-related violence, hardly more than the average daily death toll in the volatile state.
Authorities were pleased at their relative success, but still cautious.
"I would not say we have dealt the separatists a death blow," Sabharwal said. "There is still some mopping-up to do."
He expected the quality and flow of police intelligence to improve under the new government.
"The elected representatives always have very good sources of information among the local people," Sabharwal said.
